⚙️ Under the hood · Step 5 of 8 · 7 min

Measure a classifier

Confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 and the accuracy trap.

🧾 Four kinds of outcome

A spam filter checked 100 messages. Compare what it said with the truth:

Really spamReally not spam
Filter said “spam”3010
Filter said “not spam”555

30 true positives (TP), 10 false positives (FP: good mail in the spam folder), 5 false negatives (FN: spam that got through) and 55 true negatives (TN). This table is called a confusion matrix.

Task. Accuracy is the share of all answers that were right. What is the accuracy of this spam filter, in percent?

Show the solution

85 of the 100 answers were right: 85%.

Task. Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of everything the filter called spam, how much really was spam? Answer in percent.

Show the solution

30 / 40 = 75%. One in four flagged messages was a good one.

Task. Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of all the real spam, how much did the filter catch? Answer in percent, rounded to a whole number.

Show the solution

30 / 35 ≈ 85.7%, so about 86%. Five spam messages got through.

⚖️ F1: one number for both

Precision and recall pull in different directions, so they are often combined into the F1 score, their harmonic mean. It is high only when both are high.

F1 = 2·P·R / (P + R)

Task. For the filter, P = 0.75 and R = 6/7 ≈ 0.857. What is its F1 score, to two decimal places?

Show the solution

≈ 1.286 / 1.607 ≈ 0.80. In exact fractions it is 36/45 = 0.8.

Task. You raise a spam filter's threshold: now it flags a message only when it is very sure. What usually happens?

Show the answer

Right answer: Precision goes up, recall goes down

Fewer good messages are flagged (fewer FP), but more spam slips through (more FN). You pick the threshold by asking which mistake costs more.

Task. 1% of all payments are fraud. A “model” that always answers “not fraud” has which accuracy, and which recall for fraud?

Show the answer

Right answer: 99% accuracy and 0% recall

It is right about the 99% of honest payments and catches no fraud at all. On imbalanced data, accuracy alone is a trap: look at precision and recall.

Task. Which mistake is worse here?

Show the solution

When a missed case is dangerous, tune for recall. When a false alarm hurts someone, tune for precision. Choosing the metric is a decision about people, not only about maths.

Task. Why must the test set stay untouched until the very end?

Show the answer

Right answer: Every choice you make by looking at it leaks its information into the model

Tune on a separate validation set. Once you tune on the test set, its score is no longer an honest estimate of how the model does on new data.

Remember

  • Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all, Precision = TP / (TP + FP), Recall = TP / (TP + FN).
  • F1 = 2·P·R / (P + R): high only when both are high.
  • The threshold trades precision for recall.
  • On imbalanced data, accuracy misleads.
  • Keep the test set untouched until the end.
